title: How Painting Heals — The Art of Slowing Down
excerpt: Why picking up a brush is one of the most powerful things you can do for your mind. The science behind art and well-being, and what I've learned from years at the easel.
body:
There is a moment, maybe ten minutes into a painting, when the world outside the studio disappears. The phone stops existing. The to-do list dissolves. All that remains is the color on the brush and the surface waiting to receive it.

This is not poetry — it is neuroscience. Researchers at Drexel University found that just 45 minutes of creative activity significantly lowers cortisol, the body's primary stress hormone. It did not matter whether the participants were experienced artists or complete beginners. The act of making — of mixing pigment, choosing a stroke, committing color to canvas — activates the brain's reward pathways and quiets the default mode network, the part of the mind responsible for rumination and worry.

I have painted since I was a girl in Palermo, and I can tell you that the research matches the experience perfectly. On days when anxiety sits heavy in my chest, I do not reach for my phone. I reach for my acrylics. There is something about the physicality of paint — the resistance of the brush against canvas, the slow blending of cadmium yellow into burnt sienna — that grounds you in your body.

The American Art Therapy Association reports that around 75 percent of people experience improved emotional well-being after engaging in art-based activities. The key is that art provides a non-verbal channel for processing emotions that words cannot always reach. You do not need to name the feeling. You just need to give it a color.

What I tell anyone who asks how to begin: start with three colors and a cheap canvas. Do not aim for beauty. Aim for presence. Mix the colors slowly. Watch what happens when blue meets orange. Feel the brush move. That is the entire practice.

In Sicily, we have a phrase — piano piano — which means slowly, slowly. It is how we cook, how we garden, and how we paint. In a world that rewards speed, the brush teaches you that the richest things unfold at the pace of patience.

Painting will not solve your problems. But it will give you forty-five minutes where the problems cannot reach you. And sometimes, that is enough to change the shape of a day.
author: Milly Farfalla
